newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: Guiana remains tense after new wave of violence.
newsitem.headline: Guiana remains tense after new wave of violence.

text.p: French Guiana remained tense as night fell on Monday after a new wave of violence in the last two weeks rocked France's South Amerian territory, witnesses said.
Hundreds of para-military riot police reinforcements flown in from mainland France patrol the streets and guard key government buildings in the capital Cayenne.

Earlier on Monday, Jean Ballandras a senior government official in the French overseas department, said that while the situation remained tense it was not explosive and suggested the worst may be over.

"The sitution is strained but not a powder keg. Guiana has been through some moments of heavy tension but we are no longer there," Ballandras told a news conference. "The proof is that the last three night have been peaceful," he said.
The unrest was triggered by the arrest and transfer last week to the French Caribbean island of Martinique of 10 persons including four leading members of French Guiana's independence movement.

They were charged with arson and violence against a magistrate stemming from an attack on the residence of French Guiana's state prosecutor during an earlier wave of riots last November that left one looter dead and millions of property damage, mostly to government buildings.
Three nights of ferocious rioting left 11 police wounded including 10 by gunfire.

Police clashed with armed and hooded demonstrators in the city's centre and fired teargas to disperse crowds. Rioters fired hunting rifles and hurled Molotov cocktail firebombs. Looters ransacked stores. Those owned by ethnic Chinese were hardest hit.
The riots have shattered French Guiana's tranquil facade and laid bare economic, political and social woes.
French Guiana is the only non-independent territory on the mainland of the Western Hemisphere.
It lags behind mainland France in housing, education and health. Its economy is heavily dependent on subsidies from France and 23 percent of the population of 150,000 is unemployed.
Hardest hit are young people under 25 who represent over 50 percent of the population.
